Those handed their record in the right hand read it themselves and are not shortchanged by the thinnest measure. The second ayah then carries a blindness forward. What was refused here is not corrected there, and the distance is described as increasing rather than staying fixed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that has already described a record fastened to every person's neck and handed over to be read. The commentators report no particular occasion. They note that the ayah answers a live Meccan objection about tribal belonging, since a society organised entirely by lineage assumed that whatever happened would happen to a group, and the passage grants the group while changing what defines it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers whoever or whatever stands in front and is followed. The classical readings run from the prophet of an age to the written record of a life, and the commentators lay out the range without settling it.
The hair-thin fibre running along the groove of a date pit. The Quran uses it three times for the smallest imaginable quantity, always in denying that anyone will be wronged by even that much.

Used twice in the second ayah, of this life and the next. The commentators are unanimous that the blindness meant is of the heart rather than the eye, since the passage is about seeing what is in front of you.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca a person was called by their lineage before their name, and a stranger's first question was whose son you were. Standing, protection and blame all attached to the group, and a man punished for something his cousin did would have thought the arrangement normal. Dates were the staple food, and everyone had split a pit and seen the pale thread inside it, the most worthless thing in a household.
studies.didYouKnow: The date-stone thread appears three times in the Quran and always in the same construction: a denial that anyone will be wronged by so much as that. Two of the three occur in one surah, within a few pages of each other. The Quran also uses two other parts of a date pit for the same purpose elsewhere, the notch and the skin.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah keeps the group and changes its basis. People are still called in company, so belonging is real, but what gathers them is what they followed rather than who they were born to. That converts an inherited identity into a chosen one. The second ayah then makes a claim about continuity: the condition a person is in here is carried across rather than reset, which is why the Quran treats the present moment as the place where the outcome is being formed.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the record earlier in this surah and has each person read their own account.
Shows the one given the record in his right hand inviting others to read it too.
Explains the blindness raised on that Day by the forgetting of signs that were given here.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself who you would be called with. Not who you admire, who you actually follow: whose opinions you check before forming your own, whose approval you are shaped by, whose reading of events becomes yours. Write down three names honestly. You do not have to change anything today. It is worth simply knowing whose queue you are standing in.

studies.title: Had We Not Made You Firm
studies.meaning: The pressure on the messenger is described from the inside and it is not threat but offer. They came close to drawing him off what had been revealed, so that he would produce something else and attribute it to God, and the reward on the table was friendship. Commentators are careful about the second ayah. Nothing happened; the wording says he came near to leaning a little, and that even that near miss was prevented from outside him. What is being described is the size of the pull, not a failure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years of open opposition. The classical sources report several attempts by leaders of the city to reach a negotiated settlement with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and they differ over the details of what was proposed. What the commentators agree on is the shape: repeated approaches offering standing and inclusion in exchange for some accommodation over what was being recited.

keyTerms.note: The verb of testing metal in fire, used here of a sustained attempt to work someone loose from a position. It implies patient pressure applied over time rather than a single moment of temptation.

From a word for a corner or a support you put your weight on. It describes reliance and leaning toward, not agreement, so the ayah names a shift in posture that would have preceded any change of position.

Not a companion but someone whose friendship has worked into you. The root suggests something that penetrates and settles inside, which is why the Quran uses it for the closest bond a person can hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan politics ran through friendship rather than office. There was no ruler and no court; decisions were made by men who could bring their allies with them, and the way to change someone's position was to offer standing inside your circle. The word this ayah uses for what they were offering is the word for that bond. Isolation in such a city was not loneliness. It was the loss of every protection a person had.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for an intimate friend appears three times in the Quran, and the three sit at very different points. In one, Abraham is described as taken by God for such a friend. In another, a person on the Day of Judgement cries out in regret over the friend he chose. Here it is the price being offered for a small accommodation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that are usually kept apart. The prophet is fully human, close enough to leaning that the ayah says so plainly, and the revelation is fully protected, because the firmness came from God rather than from his own resolve. That protects the message without idealising the messenger. It also names the mechanism of compromise accurately: nobody is asked to abandon a position, only to lean slightly, and the invention would follow later.

crossReferences.why: Records the demand for a different recitation and the refusal to alter it from himself.
States the offer in one line: they would like you to soften, so that they may soften.
Says what would follow if any saying were invented and attributed to God by him.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where you have been leaning rather than moving: a standard you have not dropped but have stopped mentioning, a boundary you still hold but no longer explain. Name one this week and say it out loud to one person who would notice. The ayah is about the lean that comes before the change, which is the part that is easiest to miss.

studies.title: Double In Life And Death
studies.meaning: The sentence begun in the previous ayah reaches its consequence, and it is stated about the messenger himself. Had the lean become a change, the reckoning would have been doubled in this life and doubled in dying, and nobody would have come to his aid. Commentators read the doubling as proportion rather than severity for its own sake: the same act weighs more when done by the person carrying the message, because more depends on it. The ayah is a warning delivered as reassurance, since it explains why the firmness was given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage about attempts to negotiate over what was being recited. The commentators note that this is one of a small number of places where a consequence is set out conditionally for the Prophet himself, and that these passages were recited publicly in a city looking for evidence that he was inventing the message. A man composing his own revelation does not compose this.

keyTerms.note: The word for something folded over on itself, so a portion counted twice. The Quran uses the same root for multiplied reward, which means the doubling here is the ordinary rule of proportion running in the other direction.

keyTerms.gloss: We would have made you taste
keyTerms.note: The verb of tasting, used across the Quran for undergoing a consequence directly rather than hearing of it. It makes the experience personal and immediate, closing the distance a warning usually keeps.
One who comes to your aid when you are outmatched, in the specific sense of taking your side in a conflict. The denial is not that help would be refused but that no such party exists in this case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia the standing of the wrongdoer changed the weight of the wrong. A chief who broke a guarantee of safe conduct damaged more than a stranger doing the same, because the guarantee was worth exactly what his word was worth, and everyone travelling under it was exposed at once. The audience understood a scale that rose with responsibility. This ayah applies that familiar rule at the highest point of the scale.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah closes three separate ayat with almost the same clause: then you would find nobody for yourself against Us. Each time the missing figure is named with a different word. In one it is a kinsman who pursues a claim, in another a helper who takes your side, in the third a guardian who answers for you. Three offices, all absent.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Proportion is the principle at work, and it cuts against a common assumption about closeness to God. Nearness raises exposure rather than lowering it, because the person who carries a trust can damage more by mishandling it. The passage also does something for the reader's confidence in the text. A message that turns its severest conditional statement on its own bearer is not being shaped to serve him, which is part of why these ayat were preserved and recited.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same doubling to the Prophet's household, for the same reason of proximity.
States the same conditional in stronger terms, with none of you able to shield him.
Has him say he fears the punishment of a great Day if he disobeyed his Lord.

studies.applyIt: Consider one place where people rely on your word more than you usually remember: a team, a child, a friend who quotes you. Pick a small commitment you have been letting slide there and keep it exactly this week. Not because the stakes are dramatic, but because the weight of a promise really does scale with how many people are standing on it.

studies.title: No Change In Our Way
studies.meaning: The pressure described earlier turns into a plan to remove him from the land altogether, and the ayah answers with a timetable rather than a threat. Had they succeeded, they would not have remained long behind him. Then the case is widened: this is how it has gone with the messengers sent before, and the pattern itself is stated to be unalterable. Commentators read the second ayah as the ground of the first. The outcome is not a prediction about Mecca but the application of a rule.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing years before the emigration, when the leadership of the city was actively considering how to be rid of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The commentators note the wording is about expulsion rather than killing, and read the passage as spoken while that plan was still forming. Read afterwards, the ayah acquired a second life, since the emigration did take place and the outcome it names did follow.

keyTerms.note: The word for a track worn by repeated passage, so a path made by use rather than by decree. Applied to God's dealings it names regularity in history: not a rule announced, but a shape the record keeps taking.
The verb for staying on in a place after others have gone. It measures duration rather than survival, so the ayah speaks about how long the arrangement would hold rather than about anybody's death.

Moving a thing from one state or place to another. The same word appears earlier in this surah, where the objects people invoke are said to be unable to shift a hardship, and here where nobody can shift God's way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction an Arabian town could impose short of killing. A man put outside the protection of his people could be robbed on the road with no one to answer for it, and his family lost their standing with him. It was used precisely because it did not break the taboo on shedding kindred blood inside the sanctuary. Driving someone out looked like the safe option, which is what this ayah is addressing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for shifting something out of place occurs three times in the Quran, and two of those are in this surah, roughly twenty ayat apart. In the first, the things people invoke cannot shift a hardship off them. In the second, nobody can shift the way God deals with communities. The same inability is stated of the false object and of the human objector.
studies.theologicalSignificance: History is presented as regular rather than as a series of unrelated interventions, which is why the surah keeps returning to earlier peoples. That regularity does two things at once. It makes the record of the past evidence about the present, and it removes God's dealings from the reach of negotiation, since a way that cannot be shifted also cannot be bargained with. What looks like a warning to Mecca is, in the second ayah, a statement about the structure of time.

crossReferences.why: Repeats that no alteration will be found in the way God has always dealt with people.
Says the same in stronger terms, that this way admits neither alteration nor turning aside.
Records the plotting to detain, kill or expel him, and the counter-plan set against it.

studies.applyIt: Look at a pattern in your own life that has repeated three or four times: the same argument, the same job ending, the same friendship cooling. Write the repetitions in a line on one page. Patterns are visible from a distance and invisible up close, and the useful part is not the explanation. It is seeing the shape at all.

studies.title: From The Sun's Decline
studies.meaning: Prayer is fixed to the sky rather than to a clock. One span runs from the sun's turn until the night thickens, and the dawn recitation is named separately. Commentators differ over where the first span begins, most reading the sun's decline from its height, some reading its setting, and the tradition has understood the whole ayah to establish the daily times. The last clause gives the dawn its own character. That recitation is described as attended, and the classical readings take the witnesses to be angels.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah largely occupied with rejection and argument. The commentators note the shift: after pages of dispute, an instruction arrives that is not addressed to the objectors at all. Prayer had been part of the community's life from early in the Meccan period, and this ayah is read as marking out its times rather than introducing the practice for the first time.

keyTerms.note: A word for the sun moving off its highest point and beginning to slide. The classical commentators divide over whether it marks noon or sunset, and both readings are recorded side by side without either being suppressed.
Night at the point where it has properly gathered rather than merely fallen. The noun occurs only here in the Quran, and it names a stage of the evening rather than an hour.
A passive form: something others are present at. It says nothing about who attends, and the classical readings fill that in with angels, which is why the dawn recitation is singled out from the rest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Mecca owned a clock. The day was read off the sky and off the ground, and a person told the time by where their own shadow fell and how long it had grown. Shepherds, traders and caravan masters all worked to the same natural marks, so an instruction tied to the sun's decline and the gathering of night was legible to everyone at once, in the desert as in the town, without any instrument.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the word Quran is used to name a moment of the day. The phrase is not the prayer of dawn but the recitation of dawn, and it appears twice within a single ayah, the second time to say that it is attended. The naming has carried into practice: the dawn prayer is the one traditionally recited aloud and at length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fixing worship to the movement of the sun ties a person's day to something they do not control and cannot negotiate with. The times arrive whether or not anyone is ready, which builds an external rhythm into a life rather than leaving devotion to be fitted around inclination. The final clause adds a second idea: that an act performed alone in the dark is described as attended, so privacy and witness are not opposites here.

crossReferences.why: Marks the same spans differently, at the two ends of the day and in the night's approach.
Sets the times of praise across evening, morning, late afternoon and noon in one sweep.
Pairs the times of prayer with patience under what people say, as this surah also does.

studies.applyIt: For one week, notice the sky at the time of one prayer rather than checking an app. Step outside at the point when the light changes and look up before you begin. You are not doing anything different. But the ayah ties the act to something visible, and a person who has actually watched the light go tends to arrive differently.

studies.title: Keep Vigil With It
studies.meaning: A part of the night is set aside for rising with the recitation, and it is described as something additional rather than as part of the ordinary round. The reason given is not merit but expectation: perhaps your Lord will raise you to a station that is praised. Commentators note the particle of hope, which keeps a promise from hardening into a guarantee even here. The classical tradition connects the station widely with intercession on the Day of Judgement, and reports it as such rather than deducing it from the words.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) during a period of sustained hostility. The commentators place the night vigil early in the mission, and note that a lengthy night standing was part of the first years before the pattern of the day's prayers settled. Read in sequence, the instruction arrives directly after the daily times and directly before a supplication for a true entrance and exit.

keyTerms.note: From a root that carries both sleeping and casting sleep off, so the single word contains the effort in it. The form used here means to put sleep away deliberately after having been in it.

Whatever is given over and above what is due, whether an act offered or a gift received. The word occurs twice in the Quran, once as this night standing and once as a grandson granted beyond what was asked.
A passive form from the root behind praise, so the station is defined by what others say of the one placed in it. The exact phrase occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in Arabia was long, cold and lit only by stars, and nobody wasted lamp oil on it. Households slept early because there was nothing else to do, and rising in the middle of it meant standing in the dark and the chill without company. The early Muslims kept these vigils in Mecca while under watch during the day, so the hours when the city slept were the hours when they were least observed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for something extra occurs only twice in the Quran. In the other place it describes Jacob, granted to Abraham over and above the son he had asked for. The same term therefore covers an act a person offers beyond what is required and a gift God gives beyond what was requested, running in both directions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches an outcome to a practice while refusing to make the link automatic, and the particle of hope is doing that work. It also says something about what is extra. An act described as an addition is precisely the one tied here to the highest station, which suggests that what a person does beyond obligation reveals more than what they do inside it. The reward named is standing among others rather than a private benefit.

crossReferences.why: Describes the night standing at length, and calls the impression made then stronger and truer.
Describes those who slept little of the night and sought forgiveness before the dawn.
Pictures sides parting from beds to call on their Lord in fear and hope.

studies.applyIt: If you already wake in the night, do not go straight back to sleep. Sit up for the length of a short recitation and then lie down again. If you never wake, set nothing and force nothing; simply notice that the ayah treats the extra thing as the significant one, and find one small extra thing in your day instead.

studies.title: An Entry Of Truth
studies.meaning: A prayer, a declaration, and a description. The prayer asks for an entrance and an exit that are both truthful, which the commentators read as any coming in and going out being sound at both ends, and many connect it to the migration ahead. The declaration announces that truth has arrived and falsehood is already vanishing, using a word for something that drains away. The third ayah says the same Quran works differently on different hearers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the last years there, immediately after instructions about the times of prayer and the night vigil. Many classical commentators connect the prayer about entering and leaving to the migration to Medina, and some report that the declaration about truth was spoken at the clearing of the sanctuary years later. The reports differ on the details, and the prayer is read more widely than any single occasion.

keyTerms.note: A construction that attaches truthfulness to a place or an act rather than to a statement. It asks that the coming in be honest in itself, without pretence at the start or regret at the end.
A verb used of a soul leaving the body and of something draining out. It does not mean falsehood was defeated; it means it emptied, which makes the collapse look internal rather than inflicted.
A medical word for recovery from illness. Commentators divide over whether the healing is of the heart, of doubt, or of the body, and most allow the range rather than narrowing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person entering a town in Arabia did so under someone's protection or not at all, and leaving could be as dangerous as arriving. Travellers announced themselves, named their patron, and left with an escort to the edge of safe ground. Praying for a true entrance and a true exit used the vocabulary of that arrangement. It asked for the thing every traveller wanted: to arrive without deceit and to leave without disgrace.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for healing is used of the Quran in three places, and in every one it is paired with another quality: mercy here, mercy and admonition elsewhere, guidance in another. It is never left standing alone. The final clause of this passage is also carefully phrased: the Quran is not said to cause loss, only that the wrongdoers increase in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three ayat together give a shape to living under opposition. First a prayer for integrity in what you do, then a statement about what is already true regardless of appearances, then an account of why the same message divides its hearers. The last is the theologically striking one. Nothing in the Quran changes between the believer and the wrongdoer; what changes is what it meets, and the outcome is attributed to that.

crossReferences.why: Calls the Quran an admonition, a healing for what is in the chests, guidance and mercy.
Says the same book is guidance and healing for some and obscurity for others.
Describes truth hurled against falsehood so that it is crushed and vanishes.

studies.applyIt: Say the prayer in the first of these ayat before something you are dreading this week: a meeting, a hospital visit, a conversation. Ask for an honest way in and an honest way out. Then notice, afterwards, whether you left the room the same person who walked in. That is the specific thing the prayer is asking for.

studies.title: He Turns His Side Away
studies.meaning: Two responses are put side by side and both are failures, which is the point. Given something good, the human being turns aside and puts distance between himself and the giver. Touched by hardship, he collapses into hopelessness. Neither reaction takes the event as connected to anything. The reply that follows widens rather than scolds: each acts out of the shape he has been formed into, and the assessment of who is better guided is left with God. Commentators read the second ayah as removing the reader's licence to grade anybody.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of ayat about how people receive what comes to them. The commentators report no specific occasion and read the description as general rather than aimed at named opponents. The surah has just described a rescue at sea forgotten on land, so the pattern being named here is one the passage has already shown in a particular case before stating it as a characteristic.

keyTerms.note: A verb for putting physical distance between yourself and something. Paired with the mention of his side it makes the response bodily: a shoulder turned and a step taken, rather than a thought or a denial.

An intensive form, so not disappointment but the settled conviction that nothing further will come. The Quran treats this state seriously enough to name it here as the exact counterpart of the turning away above.

From a root about shape and resemblance, so a person's formed disposition rather than their choice in a moment. It occurs only here, and the commentators read it as manner, temperament and inclination together.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's fortunes in Mecca swung within a single season. One caravan through meant a house rebuilt and marriages arranged; one caravan lost to raiders or weather meant debt and dependence on relatives. The audience had watched neighbours behave exactly as this ayah describes, unreachable in a good year and unconsolable in a bad one, and had probably done both themselves within living memory.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a person's own formation occurs only once in the whole Quran, here. Classical lexicographers connect it with a root covering both shape and likeness, and the commentators gloss it variously as nature, manner, and the road one is on. The Quran states the diversity of human make in a word it never uses again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing exposes a single fault wearing two faces. Both responses treat the event as the whole of reality, so good fortune makes God unnecessary and hardship makes Him absent, and in neither case is He part of the picture. The second ayah then does something unexpected with that diagnosis. Instead of ranking people, it hands the ranking back to God, which turns an observation about human weakness into a restraint on the reader's judgement of others.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same double portrait at length, including the turning aside when good is received.
Draws the same contrast and names the exception: those who are patient and do good.
Answers the despair directly, forbidding no one to hope in the mercy of God.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last week and find one good thing and one hard thing. Ask, honestly, whether either of them changed how much you prayed. If the good one made you lighter and the hard one made you quieter, you have the pattern this ayah describes. Try the reverse once: thank God specifically for the good thing, out loud.

studies.title: You Were Given Little
studies.meaning: A question is put and the answer withholds rather than explains. The Spirit belongs to the command of the Lord, and the questioners are told how much knowledge they hold: only a little. Commentators differ widely over what is being asked about, offering the human soul, the angel who brings revelation, revelation itself, and a great creature named in the accounts of the Day. They record the range without resolving it, which is a reasonable response to an answer that was designed not to settle the matter.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical reports say the question was put at the prompting of scholars of the earlier scriptures, who suggested it as a test, and the sources differ over whether the exchange happened in Mecca or later. What the commentators agree on is the setting: a question asked to expose a limit rather than to learn something, and answered in a way that made the limit the subject.

keyTerms.note: The definite form suggests something already known to the questioners rather than a general category. The word is used across the Quran for revelation, for the angel who carries it, and for what is breathed into a human being.

Both an order given and a matter belonging to someone. Saying the Spirit is of the Lord's affair places it in His jurisdiction rather than describing what it is, which is why the reply is not an evasion.

The word closes the ayah and applies to everyone addressed. It does not say human knowledge is worthless, only that the portion given is small, which makes the reply a measurement rather than a rebuke.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Test questions were a recognised form in that world. A visiting scholar or a rival poet would put a question with no good answer, and the audience judged the man by how he handled it rather than by whether he knew. Reputations were made and lost this way in front of a crowd. The expected move was to bluff or to change the subject, and answering by naming a limit was not the move anybody was waiting for.
studies.didYouKnow: Thirteen times the Quran uses the same formula: they ask you about something, and the reply begins with an instruction to say. The questions cover crescent moons, orphans, what to spend, the sacred month, intoxicants, the mountains and more, and nearly all receive a direct answer. Only two withhold it, this one and the repeated question about when the Hour will come.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah establishes that there is a bounded region of what human beings are given to know, and it does so inside revelation rather than against it. That protects theology from a certain kind of overreach: a scripture that answered everything would license the reader to expect an answer to everything. It also treats a small portion as a gift rather than a deprivation, since the sentence says knowledge was given, and the smallness is a description of scale.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit differently: they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills.
Measures the words of the Lord against an ocean of ink, which would run out first.
Extends that image to every tree as pens and seven seas behind them, still not exhausted.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been arguing about, online or at a table, where you are not actually informed. Say plainly to one person this week that you do not know enough about it to have a view. It is a small sentence and it costs something. Notice what it frees up in the conversation once it has been said.

studies.title: Nothing But A Mercy
studies.meaning: A possibility is raised that nobody had raised: what was revealed could be taken back, and there would be no one to appeal to about it. The exception in the next ayah is the whole passage. Only a mercy from the Lord stands between the Prophet and that removal, and the sentence closes by calling the favour already shown him great. Commentators read the pair as addressed to a man who had just been told he was nearly drawn off the message, and note that the security offered is a relationship rather than a possession.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the passage about attempts to negotiate over the recitation and the statement that firmness had been given from outside. The commentators place these ayat within the same sequence and read them as its conclusion: the message was kept, the keeping was not the messenger's doing, and both facts are stated to him plainly rather than withheld for his comfort.

keyTerms.note: The emphatic form of a plain verb meaning to go with something, to carry it off. The construction is deliberately unremarkable, which makes the removal sound as easy as picking something up and leaving.

Indefinite here, so a mercy rather than the mercy. Grammar makes it an act freely given in this instance rather than a standing entitlement, which is why the sentence following it speaks of favour rather than of right.
What is given beyond any claim. Naming it after the possibility of removal reframes what is held: the revelation is described as surplus received rather than as property secured.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Memory was the library of that world. Poetry, genealogy and treaty terms lived in trained memories and nowhere else, and a tribe that lost its reciter lost its history within a generation. People understood exactly how fragile a body of words was and how completely it could vanish. To an audience with no archives, the idea of a revelation being carried away was not an abstraction but the ordinary fate of everything spoken.
studies.didYouKnow: Every ayah of this surah but one closes on the same sound, a long open vowel, so the whole chapter chimes from beginning to end and a listener can hear where each ayah stops without knowing the words. The single exception is its opening ayah, which ends instead on two names of God, the Hearing and the Seeing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as held rather than owned, and that changes the relationship a person can have with it. Nobody, including the one who received it, has a claim on continued access, so the appropriate posture toward scripture is gratitude rather than assurance. The passage also completes something begun earlier. The firmness that kept him from leaning and the mercy that keeps the revelation with him are the same thing described twice, from the inside and from the outside.

crossReferences.why: Names the firmness given from outside him, which this passage identifies as a mercy.
States the other side of the same arrangement: the reminder was sent down and is guarded.
Answers a fear of exactly this kind, saying the Lord has neither forsaken nor detested him.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you have stopped being grateful for because you assume it will still be there tomorrow: your eyesight, a language you can read, the ability to remember your own childhood. Choose one and use it deliberately today while noticing that you are using it. Assurance and gratitude tend to occupy the same space, and only one of them fits at a time.

studies.title: Even Backing One Another
studies.meaning: A challenge is issued in the widest possible terms. Humankind and the unseen creatures together, working as allies rather than separately, could not bring the like of this recitation. Commentators note two features of the wording. The pooling of effort is granted in advance, so the failure cannot be blamed on isolation, and the challenge is not to write something good but to produce the like of this, which leaves the standard of comparison in the text itself rather than in anybody's judgement.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience that valued composed speech more than almost anything else. Poetry was the public art of Arabia and the finest poets were known across the peninsula. The commentators note the challenge was made repeatedly and in narrowing forms across the Meccan and Medinan periods, and that it was made in the open, to people who had every reason to answer it.

keyTerms.note: A form implying deliberate assembly for a shared purpose, not a crowd happening to be in one place. The verb concedes to the challenged party the one advantage they might otherwise have claimed was missing.
Likeness, not equality of quality. The demand is for something of the same kind rather than for something as good, which is a narrower and more testable request than a general comparison would be.

From the word for a back. It names the person who stands behind you in a dispute and lends weight, so the phrase pictures the two groups propping each other up rather than merely working side by side.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia judged speech competitively and in public. Poets held recognised rank, their verses were memorised by people who could not read, and a tribe's standing rose with the reputation of its best voice. Composition was tested at seasonal gatherings where audiences knew the forms well enough to catch a weak line. A challenge to produce comparable speech was not rhetorical in that setting. It was an invitation into the one contest the city knew how to run.
studies.didYouKnow: The same challenge appears four times in the Quran, and the scale changes each time. One passage asks for something like the whole Quran, another for ten surahs, and two more for a single surah. Read in the order of their revelation, the demand narrows steadily while the answer stays the same, which is a pattern the classical commentators noticed early.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage stakes the claim of revelation on something publicly testable rather than on private experience, which is unusual. Anyone can attempt it and the attempt can be judged by an audience. Including the unseen creatures also closes off an escape: the challenge is not merely to human capability but to created capability as such. What the Quran offers as evidence for itself is, in the end, itself.

crossReferences.why: Narrows the same challenge to a single surah, and invites witnesses to be called in.
Sets the demand at ten surahs and offers the objectors any help they can find.
Answers the charge of invention by asking them simply to bring a statement like it.

studies.applyIt: Read one page of the Quran aloud in Arabic this week even if you do not follow the meaning, and listen to it as sound. Then read a page of any other book aloud straight after. You are not proving anything by doing this. You are simply putting yourself in the position of the first audience, who judged with their ears.

studies.title: A Spring From The Ground
studies.meaning: Every kind of comparison has been turned over for people in this recitation, and most still refuse. Then the refusal states its own terms, and the list begins: make a spring burst out of the ground for us, or own a garden of palms and vines with rivers driven through it. Commentators note what the demands have in common. They are not requests for evidence but for a different life, and each one names something the objectors themselves would have wanted, so the test proposed is really a description of what they value.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the period of settled opposition. The classical sources report a delegation of leading men putting a list of conditions to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and while the reports differ over who was present and what exactly was said, they agree on the form: a set of demands offered as the price of belief. The surah records the list without abbreviating it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning something over so its different faces show, used of wind changing direction. Applied to comparisons it means the same truth presented from many angles rather than many separate truths.

A source that rises on its own rather than a well that is dug. It occurs only here in the Quran, and in a country where water was reached by digging, a spring appearing unaided was the most valuable thing imaginable.

The word for the gaps between things, so watercourses running between the trunks rather than around the plot. The detail makes the demand specific: not a garden with water nearby, but water threaded through it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no farmland. It sat in a bare valley and lived on trade and on the well at the sanctuary, while the date gardens and vines belonged to Taif in the hills and to the oases north of the city. Wealthy Meccans bought produce from those places or held property there. The garden being demanded here was a real and specific object of envy, held by other people in another town.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a spring that rises of its own accord occurs only once in the entire Quran, in this demand. The Quran elsewhere describes water gushing from rock, springs opened in the earth, and rivers running beneath gardens, but the particular noun the objectors reach for here is never used again, in any context.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the failure of comparison and the demand for miracles in the same breath, which is an argument rather than a sequence. What was offered was many angles on one truth; what was asked for was a spectacle. The list also reveals a confusion the Quran treats as central: signs are being valued as goods rather than read as signs, so the objectors ask for the thing itself instead of what it would point to.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same appetite by saying a sign could be brought and would not settle anything.
Records the parallel list of demands, including the treasure and the garden to eat from.
Explains earlier in this surah why signs of that order were not being sent to them.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you would accept as proof about a decision you are avoiding. Write the condition down in one sentence, exactly as you would state it. Then read it back and ask whether, if it happened tomorrow, you would actually act. Most conditions of that kind are not tests. They are ways of postponing, and seeing that written down is usually enough.

studies.title: Bring Them Face To Face
studies.meaning: The demands escalate from things a wealthy man might have to things nobody could have. Bring the sky down on us in fragments, as you have been claiming will happen, or produce God and the angels here in front of us. Commentators note the first phrase, which shows the objectors could repeat the warning accurately and were asking for the threatened event as a demonstration. The second asks for the unseen to be made a witness on the spot, which would end the situation the demand is trying to leverage.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of the list of conditions put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The commentators note that a request to see angels appears repeatedly in the Meccan surahs, sometimes as a demand for a messenger who was an angel, sometimes as a demand that angels be sent down as witnesses. The answers given are consistent, and none of them grants the request.

keyTerms.note: Fragments broken from something larger, used elsewhere for pieces of cloud. It makes the demand physical rather than poetic: not the sky falling as an image, but slabs of it coming down on their heads.

A verb used for a claim the speaker does not accept. Arabic writers describe it as the word you reach for when reporting something you consider unfounded, so the objection is carried in the verb itself.
The classical commentators read it as both a group brought before them and a guarantor standing opposite. The two senses agree on the essential demand: the unseen made present and answerable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian agreements were sealed by a guarantor standing physically present. A man who vouched for a debt or a truce attended the meeting so that both parties could see him and later name him, because there were no written contracts to fall back on. Asking for God and the angels to be brought as surety uses that exact procedure. The objectors were demanding the ordinary legal form of their world be applied to the unseen.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand to see angels recurs across the Meccan surahs, and the Quran answers it in more than one way. One passage says angels come down only with the truth, and that if they came the matter would be settled at once. Another states that the day people see them will be no good news for those who denied. The request is never simply refused; it is described as one they would not survive.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The demand exposes a misunderstanding about how belief works. What is being asked for would remove the condition under which belief has any meaning, since a guarantor standing in front of you produces compliance rather than trust. The Quran consistently treats the veil over the unseen as part of the arrangement rather than an obstacle to it. Faith is asked for in a world where the evidence is real but not overwhelming, and this passage says why.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand, saying angels descend only with the truth and no respite follows.
Records the demand to see angels and calls the day they are seen no good news.
Explains that sending an angel would have ended the matter, with no reprieve given afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you tell yourself would settle a doubt, and then imagine having it: the outcome guaranteed, the answer confirmed, no room left to wonder. Sit with that for a minute. Most people find they would lose something they wanted to keep. Trust and certainty are different goods, and this week is a good time to notice which one you are actually after.

studies.title: Only A Human Messenger
studies.meaning: The list finishes with a house of ornamented gold and an ascent into the sky, and then the objectors concede their own game: even if he climbed, they would not believe the climb unless he came back with a book they could read. Commentators note that the last condition undoes all the others, since it admits that no display would be enough. The reply is one line and it declines every item. It does not argue, it declares God far above such bargaining and states what the speaker is: a human being, sent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the list of conditions. The commentators note the surah has already recorded, near its opening, a night journey and an ascent, and that the objectors here are demanding an ascent with a receipt attached. Reports about the exchange differ in their details, and the sources treat the list as representative of a running argument rather than as the transcript of one meeting.

keyTerms.note: Decorative gold worked onto a surface rather than solid metal. The Quran uses the same word for the adornment the world puts on, so the demand names a house that is beautified rather than simply valuable.

The noun for the act of ascending, from a root used for going up a ladder or a slope. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the objectors use it to dismiss in advance the very thing they are asking for.
The word for a human considered as a body, from a root about skin. It is the term the Quran uses when the point is ordinariness, which is why it sits beside the word for messenger here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Mecca but was uncommon, used for contracts, debts and letters rather than for literature. A written document carried an authority speech did not, because it survived the memory of the men who made it. Demanding a book that could be read, brought down and handed over, was asking for the one form of proof their commercial world treated as final, and it came from people who mostly could not read.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the objectors use for the ascent they are demanding occurs only here in the Quran. Their final condition is also self-defeating in its own terms: they ask for a climb into the sky and then say in advance that the climb alone would not persuade them, so the demand they end on cancels the whole list they have just recited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes something the tradition has held onto ever since: the messenger is a human being and nothing more, and the message is not authenticated by his becoming something else. That closes the door on treating him as a wonder-worker whose credentials are displays, and it keeps the argument where the Quran wants it, on the recitation itself. The exclamation of God's transcendence at the head of the reply also refuses the frame, since bargaining assumes a party who can be bargained with.

crossReferences.why: Has him say the same thing in almost the same words: I am only a human being like you.
Repeats the declaration and adds what follows from it, that he is told what to say.
Lists what he does not claim: treasuries, the unseen, being an angel, only what is revealed.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much easier it is to admire someone from a distance than to take their advice up close. Pick a person whose ordinariness you know too well, a parent, a sibling, an old friend, and take one thing they have said seriously this week. The passage is about what people demand before they will listen, and most of those demands are about status.

studies.title: If Angels Walked The Earth
studies.meaning: One objection is isolated as the whole obstacle: guidance arrived, and what stopped people was the question of whether God would send a human being as a messenger. The answer is a proportion rather than a rebuke. Had the earth been settled by angels going about at ease, an angel would have been sent down to them. Commentators read this as making the form of a messenger a matter of fit. A message is sent in the shape of those who must receive it, so the human messenger follows from the human audience.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, gathering up an objection that runs through the whole surah. The commentators note that opponents repeatedly asked why an angel had not been sent, or why an angel did not accompany him as a witness, and that the demand appears in similar words across the Meccan surahs. No single occasion is reported for this ayah; it belongs to the standing argument rather than to an incident.

keyTerms.note: The word for a human considered physically, as skin and body. The objection is carried in the choice of word, since it presses on the ordinariness of the messenger rather than on anything he said.
From a root about coming to rest after motion, used of a heart at peace and of ground that has stopped shifting. Applied to inhabitants it means dwelling as residents, not passing through.

Definite, so a particular guidance that arrived rather than direction in general. Placing it before the objection makes the sequence clear: the thing was received, and then a reason was found not to take it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society dealt through people who could be checked. An envoy between tribes was chosen because both sides knew his family and could hold his kin answerable, and a stranger with no traceable lineage was not sent on anything that mattered. That is exactly why the objectors' complaint had force among them, and exactly why the answer is about fit: a message that has to be lived out must come through someone whose life can be watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran answers the demand for an angel messenger in several different ways across the Meccan surahs. One passage says that had an angel been sent, he would have been made a man anyway, returning the objectors to their original difficulty. Another says that angels are not sent except with the decisive matter, after which no delay is granted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes a principle about revelation: it is fitted to its recipients rather than delivered in its own highest form. That has a consequence the tradition has drawn out ever since. A human messenger can be imitated, and a life lived under the same conditions as the audience becomes part of the message rather than a concession to weakness. It also removes a hidden assumption in the objection, that grandeur is evidence and ordinariness is not.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand by noting that an angel sent would have been made a man anyway.
States that every messenger before him also ate food and walked in the markets.
Records messengers agreeing they are only human, while insisting God favours whom He wills.

studies.applyIt: Think about a piece of good advice you dismissed because of the source: too young, too close, too much like you. The objection in this ayah is exactly that one, scaled up. Go back to the advice this week and consider it on its own, separated from whoever gave it, and see whether it survives.

studies.title: Enough As A Witness
studies.meaning: After a long argument the dispute is handed to a third party, and the third party is God. The wording is a settled Arabic formula for saying that no further testimony is needed. Two descriptions follow and they are not decorative. He is inwardly acquainted with His servants and He sees them, which covers what a person hides and what a person does. Commentators note that this ends the exchange without conceding anything and without claiming victory, since a witness is invoked precisely where argument has stopped being useful.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a long stretch of demands and refusals. The commentators read it as marking the point where the case had been made and repeated and would not be made again. In a society without courts or written contracts, an appeal to witnesses was the ordinary way a dispute was concluded, so the formula would have registered as procedural rather than as a rhetorical flourish.

keyTerms.note: The verb states adequacy rather than superiority. It does not say God is the best witness available; it says no other is needed, which closes the matter rather than winning it.
From a root about probing something to learn what is under the surface. It names knowledge of the hidden side of a matter, which is why it is paired here with a word for plain seeing.
Sight of what is open and visible. Set beside the previous word it divides the field between what is concealed and what is displayed, so that nothing is left in either category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every serious transaction in Mecca needed witnesses. Sales, marriages, debts and truces were held together by named men who had been present and could be produced later, and a claim without them was hard to press. Witnesses were chosen for standing, since their word would be weighed against another's. Invoking a witness whose knowledge reached inside a person removed the one weakness the system had, which was that witnesses only saw the outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula saying God suffices as a witness recurs across the Quran, and it usually appears at the end of a dispute rather than in the middle of one. It is used between a messenger and those refusing him, between parties to an agreement, and once about what God Himself has sent down. The construction is the same each time and the function is closure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Calling a witness rather than pressing the argument says something about what the disagreement was. Both parties had heard everything; what separated them was not information. The two names then locate the real record. Since one covers the hidden and the other the visible, the testimony being invoked includes what each side knew privately about its own honesty, which is a far more uncomfortable court than a public one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula to close a passage about where good and harm come from.
Answers the charge that he was not sent by calling God a sufficient witness between them.
Repeats the formula and adds that He knows what is in the heavens and the earth.

studies.applyIt: Think of an argument you keep replaying, where you are certain you are right and the other person is not going to agree. Try saying to yourself, once, that God knows what actually happened. Then stop rehearsing it. You are not conceding the point. You are handing the record to someone who already has it.

studies.title: Whoever God Guides
studies.meaning: Guidance is described as something received rather than achieved, and the one guided is named by the fact of it rather than by any quality of his own. The other side is stated without softening, and then the gathering is described: brought together on their faces, without sight, speech or hearing. Commentators generally read the loss of the three faculties as corresponding to how they were used here. The last clause is the hardest. Whenever the fire settles, it is raised again, so even the exhaustion of a punishment is withheld.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the long argument with the objectors of the city. The commentators note the surah has already described the same people listening intently while their hearts were covered and their ears weighted. That earlier description is what makes this one legible: the faculties named here are the ones named there, and the passage is following a condition through to its end.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a form meaning to receive guidance and take it up. It holds both sides together: something was given, and something was accepted, so the word is neither purely passive nor a claim of self-direction.
Used of a fire whose flame drops and whose heat falls away as fuel runs out. The verb is ordinary and domestic, which is what makes the clause that follows it land.
A fire that has been kindled up rather than one merely burning. The word implies active stoking, so it answers the previous verb exactly: what subsides on its own is raised again deliberately.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire was work. A household fire had to be fed through the night or it went out, and someone rose in the cold to push the embers together and add fuel. Everyone had watched a fire die down and knew that leaving it alone was enough to end it. The image in the last clause takes that familiar arithmetic and reverses it, which is why it needed no explanation to the first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The three faculties named here appear elsewhere in the Quran as a set, and the order is reversed. In two passages of the second surah the description runs deaf, dumb, blind, of people in this life who will not return. Here it runs blind, dumb, deaf, of the same kind of people at the gathering. The same three words, turned end to end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah holds two things that are difficult to hold together. Guidance is entirely a gift, so no one can claim it as an achievement, and the loss of it is described in terms that match how the faculties were used, so no one is treated arbitrarily. The commentators keep both by reading the leaving astray as following on a person's own turning. What the passage refuses is the middle position where a person guides himself.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same faculties being closed earlier in this surah, in the present life.
Gives the same three words in the reverse order, of people who will not turn back.
Explains the blindness at the gathering as answering the forgetting of signs received here.

studies.applyIt: If you have ever been given a direction you did not work out for yourself, a book that arrived at the right moment, a person who said the one thing you needed, take a minute today to call it what it was. Not luck and not your own judgement. Guidance is described here as received, and receiving is something you can at least notice.

studies.title: That Is Their Repayment
studies.meaning: A verdict is given a ground, and the ground has two parts joined as one: they rejected the signs, and they said this particular sentence about bones and fragments. Commentators note that the objection is quoted rather than summarised, and that it appears here word for word as it appeared earlier in the surah. The passage does not add an argument against it. It has already answered the question twice, and this time it simply lets the sentence stand as the reason, which is a different kind of reply.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators place this at the close of the surah's long engagement with the objectors, and note the structure: the same words that opened the dispute over resurrection are repeated as it ends. Denial of bodily resurrection was the most persistent Meccan objection, and it is the one the surah returns to when it is finished arguing.

keyTerms.note: From a root about settling an account, so a payment that matches rather than a penalty chosen by a judge. It is used for reward as often as for punishment, which keeps the idea of correspondence rather than severity.

The last part of a body to survive, and in Arabia the part actually seen when old ground was disturbed. The objection is built on observation, which is why the Quran answers it by moving to the question of origination.
The noun of the act of creating, used here with the word for new. The objectors are conceding that they were created once; the whole dispute is about whether that act can be performed a second time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing in a Meccan life encouraged belief in bodily return. Bodies were buried shallow in dry ground, and animal remains lay in the open along every route out of the city until they were bones and then nothing. Wealth, standing and the memory of a name were what a person could actually leave behind, and the objection recorded here was, on the evidence available, the reasonable position.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for crumbled fragments occurs only twice in the whole Quran, and both are in this surah. Arabic has many words for dust and remains; the one the objectors reached for is not used anywhere else in the text, in any speaker's mouth. The Quran keeps their vocabulary rather than translating the objection into its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a quoted objection where a reason should stand makes a claim about what refusal consists of. The wrong was not an intellectual failure but a settled use of a sentence, repeated until it did the work of thought. The verdict then follows from the words themselves. This is why the Quran so often quotes its opponents at length rather than paraphrasing them: the record of what was said is treated as the substance of the matter.

crossReferences.why: Gives this objection in identical words earlier in the surah, with the reply that answers it.
Answers the same question about crumbling bones by naming the one who produced them first.
Records the same objection and adds that their fathers had been promised this before them.

studies.applyIt: Listen for a sentence you repeat about yourself, the one that comes out whenever a certain subject arises. I am not good with people. I have never been able to save. Say it once, out loud, and hear it as a sentence rather than a fact. Repeated words start doing the work of thinking, which is the pattern this ayah is recording.

studies.title: Able To Create Their Like
studies.meaning: The argument shifts scale. Whoever made the heavens and the earth is able to make the like of these objectors, which is a smaller act than the one already granted. Commentators note the comparison is not between the first creation and the second, but between the universe and a human being, so the question of difficulty collapses. A term is then fixed for them about which there is no doubt, and the closing clause reports the outcome plainly: the wrongdoers refuse anything but denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering the objection quoted in the previous ayah. The commentators treat the argument from the greater to the lesser as one of the surah's recurring moves, and note that it appears in similar form across the Meccan period, always addressed to people who accepted that God made the heavens and the earth while denying that He could remake them.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a root about measuring and determining a quantity, not about raw force. Power in this word is the ability to set an exact amount, which is why it fits an argument about proportion.
A fixed period with a named end, used in Arabic contracts for the date a debt falls due. The commercial sense is present here: a term set by someone else, arriving whether or not the debtor is ready.
Not simple uncertainty but the doubt that disturbs and will not rest. Denying it of the term says the appointment is not the kind of thing that can be argued into vagueness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on terms. A loan was taken against the return of a caravan, and the date was named in front of witnesses because everything depended on it: the goods, the marriage arranged on the proceeds, the standing of the family. Everyone in the audience had lived under a fixed term they could not move. The word this ayah uses for the appointment is the one they used for those dates.
studies.didYouKnow: The argument from the greater creation to the smaller recurs across the Quran, and one passage states it as a bare comparison: the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of humankind, though most people do not know it. The Quran repeatedly answers doubts about resurrection by pointing at the sky rather than at the grave.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats scale as an argument, which assumes something about God that the objectors had already conceded. Once creation is granted, difficulty is not a category that applies, so denying the smaller act while accepting the greater is incoherent rather than cautious. The fixed term then adds what argument alone cannot: the matter is not only possible but scheduled, and the closing clause makes clear that what remained was never a shortage of reasons.

crossReferences.why: States the comparison directly: creating the heavens and earth is greater than creating people.
Asks the same question about the maker of the heavens and the earth creating their like.
Adds that He was not wearied by the first creation, so He can give life to the dead.

studies.applyIt: Step outside tonight and look up for one full minute without reaching for your phone. You are not being asked to feel anything in particular. The ayah makes an argument from the size of what is above you to the smallness of what worries you, and that argument only works if you have actually looked.

studies.title: Fear Of Spending
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is put to people who had been demanding treasure. Suppose you held the storehouses of my Lord's mercy: you would clutch them, out of fear of the spending itself. Commentators draw attention to the reason given. It is not fear of poverty, which would be reasonable in a finite fortune, but fear of the outgoing, which does not lessen an infinite one. The closing clause names the trait rather than the people, so the ayah is a diagnosis of the human grip rather than an accusation against one group.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the list of demands the objectors made, several of which were for wealth: a spring, a garden with rivers, a house of gold. The commentators read this ayah as turning the demand around. People asking for treasuries are shown what they would do with them, and the answer is drawn from what they were already doing with much less.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a locked store where valuables are kept back. Applied to mercy it makes an unlimited thing into something with a door, which is precisely the picture the objectors were working with.
The verb for gripping something and not letting go, used of holding water in and of restraining a hand. It describes a physical clutch rather than a policy of thrift.

An intensive form from a root about narrowing and stinting. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it names a disposition rather than an act, which is why it closes a sentence about human beings in general.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was portable and hoardable: silver, cloth, incense, stored grain. There were no banks, so a rich family kept its holdings physically, in a locked room or buried, and the storehouse was a real place with a real door. Generosity was also loudly praised in Arabian poetry, and men were remembered for slaughtering their last camel for guests. The gap between the praise and the practice is what this ayah is standing in.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a tightly closed hand occurs only once in the whole Quran. The passage also uses a construction the Quran reserves for arguments of this kind, where a person is invited to imagine holding what they have asked for. The reply is not a refusal of the request. It is a description of what the request would produce.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates the problem in the person rather than in the supply, which is a claim with wide consequences. If holding back followed from scarcity, abundance would cure it, and the Quran here says it would not. That makes generosity a matter of formation rather than of circumstance. Set against the storehouses of divine mercy, which are spent without diminishing, the contrast defines the human condition by what it does when nothing is at stake.

crossReferences.why: Says that if they had a share in dominion they would not give people even a date-stone's notch.
Names the same reluctance and observes that some withhold, and only harm themselves by it.
Sets the same trait between two limits earlier in this surah, a chained hand and an open one.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that you would not miss and have still not given away: the coat in the back of the wardrobe, the money sitting in a rounding error, the hour you keep meaning to offer someone. Notice the small resistance when you do it. That resistance is the subject of this ayah, and it is not proportional to the cost.

studies.title: Nine Clear Signs
studies.meaning: A precedent is produced. Moses was given nine signs that carried their own evidence, and the reader is directed to ask the Children of Israel, who hold the record of them. Commentators differ over the list, most naming the staff, the hand, the years of drought, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood and the shortage of crops, while some substitute other items. What is not in dispute is the outcome. Pharaoh, with all nine in front of him, said the man was under a spell.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, brought in directly after the Meccan objectors demanded signs and then declared in advance that no sign would persuade them. The commentators note the parallel is exact and deliberate: an earlier audience received the signs being demanded here, at the highest possible standard of clarity, and answered with the same word the Meccans had used a few ayat earlier.

keyTerms.note: From a root about separating one thing from another so the difference shows. A sign described this way does not require interpretation; it makes its own case, which is why the response to it is the point of the ayah.

An instruction to check with people who kept the account. It treats the Israelite record as evidence available for consultation rather than as a claim needing defence, which is a striking way to argue in a hostile setting.
A passive form: worked upon rather than working magic. It is the same charge the objectors in this surah made against the Prophet, arriving here in Pharaoh's mouth against Moses.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca knew the Israelite story through contact rather than through books. Jewish communities lived at Yathrib and in the northern oases, Meccan caravans passed through them twice a year, and the account of Moses and Pharaoh was widely enough known that it could be invoked without being retold. An instruction to go and ask was practical advice to a trading city, not a rhetorical gesture.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives the number of Moses' signs as nine in exactly two places, here and in one other surah, and it never sets out the list. The classical commentators assemble it from the plagues and wonders described elsewhere in the text, and they differ over the last two entries, which is why the tally varies between one commentary and the next.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage settles a question the objectors had raised without answering it directly. They asked for signs; the reply supplies a case where the signs were given, were clear, and changed nothing. That relocates the obstacle from evidence to willingness, which is the surah's consistent position. It also treats the histories of earlier communities as usable data rather than as edifying stories, so the past is offered here as an argument about the present.

crossReferences.why: Lists the signs sent to Pharaoh's people in sequence and records their response to each.
Records the Meccan objectors using this same word of the Prophet, earlier in this surah.
Says the signs came clear to them and were rejected out of injustice and self-importance.

studies.applyIt: Think of a claim you have not looked into because you already know what you think. Spend twenty minutes this week actually checking it with someone who holds the other view, in good faith. The ayah's instruction is simply to ask, and asking is unglamorous. It is also the only step in this passage that anybody can take.

studies.title: You Already Know
studies.meaning: The reply to Pharaoh does not argue for the signs. It tells him what he already knows, that only the Lord of the heavens and the earth sent them down, and that they came as things that give sight. Then the accusation is returned in the same grammatical shape it arrived in, with a different word at the end. The following ayah reports the outcome in a single line: he moved to drive them from the land and was drowned with everyone who went with him. Commentators note how little the text spends on the ending.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, brought in to answer objectors who had demanded signs and pre-emptively refused them. The commentators read the exchange as evidence about how refusal works at the highest level of power: not from ignorance, since the reply says he knew, but from what knowledge would have cost him. The pairing of demand, delivery and rejection is the argument the surah is making about its own audience.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a faculty of sight or a piece of evidence that produces it. Signs are described not as displays to be watched but as instruments that give the viewer vision he did not have.
A passive form from a root about being destroyed or held back from good. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it answers Pharaoh's charge with the same sentence shape and a heavier word.

The verb for startling someone out of their place. Its root occurs three times in the Quran, all in this surah, and one of the others describes the same plan being formed against the Prophet in Mecca.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was how the powerful removed a problem without a public killing. Mecca's leaders were weighing exactly that option in these years, and the surah has already said so. An audience hearing about a ruler who resolved to drive a group out of the land, and what became of him, would not have needed the parallel explained. The story was old and the plan was current.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Moses uses back at Pharaoh occurs only once in the whole Quran. The two accusations are built identically, a verb of opinion followed by a name and then a single passive participle, so the reply mirrors the charge exactly and changes only the final word. Pharaoh says bewitched; Moses says undone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply establishes that knowledge and acknowledgement are separable, which is one of the Quran's steadier claims about human beings. Pharaoh is not told he is mistaken; he is told he knows. That makes refusal a matter of what a person is willing to concede rather than what they have understood. The brevity of the ending then makes a second point. What took a lifetime to build is reported in half a sentence, and the text does not linger over it.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing outright: they rejected the signs while their own selves were convinced.
Uses the same verb of the plan to drive the Prophet from the land, earlier in this surah.
Gives the drowning at length, including the declaration made when it was already too late.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true about your own situation that you know and do not say: a habit that is costing you, a relationship you have already decided about. You do not have to act on it this week. Just say the sentence once, to yourself or to one person. The gap this passage describes is between knowing and admitting, and closing it starts with saying it out loud.

studies.title: Dwell In The Land
studies.meaning: After the drowning, an instruction is given to the people who had been held: settle in the land. Then the sentence jumps across all of history to its other end. When the promise of the Hereafter arrives, We will bring you gathered in a single mass. Commentators note the compression. One clause covers a settlement in a place and the next covers everyone brought together at the end, and nothing is said about the centuries in between, which the surah has already treated at its opening.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the account of Moses and Pharaoh that the surah has used as a precedent. The commentators connect this ayah to the opening of the surah, which described two episodes in the history of the Children of Israel in the land. The settlement promised here is the beginning of what those opening ayat then trace through to its consequences.

keyTerms.note: From a root about coming to rest and stillness, which also gives the word for tranquillity and for a home. The instruction is to stop moving, addressed to people who had been in flight.
A word covering both a promise made and the time set for it. Used of the Hereafter it makes the event an appointment already entered rather than an outcome that might follow from something.
From a root about wrapping and folding things together so they cannot be separated. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it pictures a crowd assembled without the divisions it arrived with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: To settle was the whole ambition. Arabian life divided between those who moved with their herds and those who held a place, and holding a place meant water, walls, stored grain and a name that outlasted a generation. Meccans knew what it cost, since their own city's standing rested on a settlement around a well. The instruction to dwell in the land would have been heard as the granting of everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the gathering here occurs only once in the whole Quran. It comes from the vocabulary of wrapping cloth around cloth until the layers cannot be told apart, and the Quran uses it for the assembling of people at the end. In a text with many words for crowds and gatherings, this one is used a single time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two promises are set in one sentence, and the second reframes the first. A land is given, and the giving is real, but it is bracketed by an appointment at which everyone will be brought together regardless of where they settled. That places every political fortune inside a larger frame without dismissing it. The word for the gathering does the rest of the work: distinctions people spend their history maintaining are described as folded together at the end.

crossReferences.why: Traces what followed this settlement, in two episodes given at the opening of this surah.
Describes the same inheritance of the land by people who had been held as weak.
Pictures the same gathering, with the earth levelled and not one of them left out.
